q: What happens when I export?
a: Revolution renders every frame of the sequence with every grade and effect and hands it to an encoder that writes the file. The two choices that matter most are the preset you start from and whether the size is set by a target bitrate or a constant quality; everything else has a sensible default.

q: What's on the Export page?
a: The settings column shows File Name, Location, Preset and Format, then the Video, Audio and Effects sections. Click Export to export now, or Send to Queue to collect several exports and run them later with Start Queue (`export.queue.start`).

q: Export now or Send to Queue?

q: In Premiere I'd switch to Export mode. Where is that here?
a: Click Export in the header (or File ▸ Export ▸ Media…, Ctrl+M): settings on the left, a preview in the middle, the queue on the side, like Premiere's Export mode.

q: What presets does the fork add?
a: The fork adds H.265 presets for 6.2K footage: YouTube 4K HEVC (3840×2160 Main 10, about 80 Mbps, for video sites), 6.2K Master HEVC (full size, about 200 Mbps), HEVC 4:2:2 10-bit master (about 240 Mbps, full vertical colour), Archive HEVC (software x265, constant quality 18: smallest file at high quality when time doesn't matter), Vertical 2160×3840 HEVC, and upstream's H.265 2160p 4K 10-bit. Start from the closest, change only what you need.

q: How fast does the hardware H.265 encoder export 6.2K?
a: On this machine the graphics card's video engine encodes H.265 through VA-API inside Revolution, with rendered pictures going straight into the encoder's memory: around 18–20 frames per second at 6.2K. The system ffmpeg's VA-API and x265 encoders are fallbacks (x265 is slower and often a little smaller), a safety net the fork plans to remove in Phase 7.

q: Why is software x265 there at all?

q: What does the Encoder speed setting do?
a: Encoder speed sets how much effort the video engine spends per picture: Driver default (no setting, the old behaviour), Speed (fastest level), Balanced, Quality (best, slowest). Drivers offer different numbers of levels (the AMD card 32, the Intel graphics 7), so the same choice isn't the same speed on both; the ffmpeg fallback gets the same level, x265 uses its own preset.

q: Why is Quality on the AMD card not the same as on Intel?

Drivers offer different numbers of levels (the AMD card 32, the Intel graphics 7), so the same choice isn't the same speed on both; the ffmpeg fallback gets the same level, x265 uses its own preset.

q: What happens if one GPU fails during a two-GPU export?
a: If either chip fails, the other finishes its parts; if both fail, the export runs again on one chip. A chip at less than a quarter of the other's speed is stopped after a few seconds and its part goes to the faster one (`retired`, not an error). `perf.stats` (`export.lanes`, `export.lanesNote`) shows what each chip did.

q: In Premiere I'd turn on Hardware Encoding. What's the Revolution setting?
a: For H.265 the Video section's Encoder choice: Auto (hardware if available, falling back), Hardware (VA-API) only, or Software (x265).

q: What's the difference between bitrate and constant quality?
a: A bitrate aims at a size (megabits per second): predictable, which upload sites and players like. Constant quality (CRF) spends as many bits as each moment needs: an even look, size known only afterwards. CBR keeps the same bitrate all the time and is rarely needed; VBR 1 pass (average with a ceiling) suits uploads.

q: In Premiere I'd pick VBR 1 pass. Is that here too?
a: Yes: the Bitrate Encoding list has CBR, VBR 1 pass, VBR 2 pass (H.264 only) and CRF (constant quality) with a Quality (CRF) number.

q: What is H.265 Main 10?
a: H.265 has Main (8-bit) and Main 10 (10-bit). 8 bits are plenty for SDR, but stretched over HDR's range they band, so HDR sequences (Rec. 2100 PQ or HLG working space) always export Main 10 with PQ or HLG signalling. When no encoder here can write HDR H.265, the sequence is tone-mapped and exported as 8-bit SDR instead.

When no encoder here can write HDR H.265, the sequence is tone-mapped and exported as 8-bit SDR instead.

q: Where are my own export presets saved?
a: Your presets are saved in your data folder (Preset Manager, `export.presets.save`); built-in ones come with Revolution. `export.formats` lists every format with its options, and `export.resolve` shows the settings a preset plus your changes add up to, without exporting.

q: Can I queue different ranges of the same sequence?
a: Yes: each queue item can be another preset, another sequence, or another range (whole sequence, In to Out, a custom range). Start runs them one after another as background jobs; Stop (`export.queue.stop`) stops the queue.

q: How do I stop the export queue?
a: Yes: each queue item can be another preset, another sequence, or another range (whole sequence, In to Out, a custom range). Start runs them one after another as background jobs; Stop (`export.queue.stop`) stops the queue.

q: In Premiere I'd send exports to Media Encoder. How do I do that in Revolution?
a: Click Send to Queue on the Export page (`export.queue.add`) for each file, then Start: the built-in queue encodes them one after another in the background while you keep editing on a snapshot of the project.

q: In Resolve I'd add jobs to the Render Queue. What's the equivalent?
a: Click Send to Queue on the Export page (`export.queue.add`) for each file, then Start: the built-in queue encodes them one after another in the background while you keep editing on a snapshot of the project.

q: Which preset does Quick Export use the first time?
a: Quick Export uses the last preset you used; the first time, Match Source – Adaptive High Bitrate. It writes the active sequence to a file next to the project, skipping the Export page.
